claim: Multiple brain regions are able to learn and express temporal sequences.
source: Multiple brain regions are able to learn and express temporal sequences, and this functionality is an essential component of learning and memory.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature, as indicated by citations throughout the paper.

claim: The model consists of a network of spiking neurons placed in a modular microcolumn based architecture.
source: The model consists of a network of spiking neurons placed in a modular microcolumn based architecture.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model architecture presented in the manuscript.

claim: Learning is performed via a biophysically realistic learning rule that depends on synaptic 'eligibility traces'.
source: Learning is performed via a biophysically realistic learning rule that depends on synaptic 'eligibility traces'.
evidence: The manuscript describes the learning rule used in the model and provides mathematical formulations.

claim: Before training, the network contains no memory of any particular sequence.
source: Before training, the network contains no memory of any particular sequence.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 3b.

claim: After training, presentation of only the first element in that sequence is sufficient for the network to recall an entire learned representation of the sequence.
source: After training, presentation of only the first element in that sequence is sufficient for the network to recall an entire learned representation of the sequence.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3e and Figure 7d.

claim: An extended version of the model demonstrates the ability to successfully learn and recall non-Markovian sequences.
source: An extended version of the model also demonstrates the ability to successfully learn and recall non-Markovian sequences.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Learned representations of temporal sequences can exist in cortical circuits.
source: Recent evidence has shown that such learned representations can exist in cortical circuits (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Xu et al., 2012; Cooke et al., 2015; Eagleman and Dragoi, 2012; Yin et al., 2008), begging the question: through what sort of circuits and learning paradigms can these representations arise?
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The parts of the model's construction are based upon recent experimental observations in visual cortex.
source: Although the parts of the model's construction are based upon recent experimental observations in visual cortex (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Xu et al., 2012; Cooke et al., 2015), utilizing observed cell types (Shuler and Bear, 2006; Liu et al., 2015; Chubykin et al., 2013) and laminar structure (Potjans and Diesmann, 2014; Binzegger et al., 2009), many of its key aspects (modularity, heterogenous representations) are illustrative of general principles of sequence learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model utilizes observed cell types from visual cortex.
source: Although the parts of the model's construction are based upon recent experimental observations in visual cortex (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Xu et al., 2012; Cooke et al., 2015), utilizing observed cell types (Shuler and Bear, 2006; Liu et al., 2015; Chubykin et al., 2013) and laminar structure (Potjans and Diesmann, 2014; Binzegger et al., 2009), many of its key aspects (modularity, heterogenous representations) are illustrative of general principles of sequence learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model utilizes laminar structure observed in cortex.
source: Although the parts of the model's construction are based upon recent experimental observations in visual cortex (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Xu et al., 2012; Cooke et al., 2015), utilizing observed cell types (Shuler and Bear, 2006; Liu et al., 2015; Chubykin et al., 2013) and laminar structure (Potjans and Diesmann, 2014; Binzegger et al., 2009), many of its key aspects (modularity, heterogenous representations) are illustrative of general principles of sequence learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The ability of the network to internally learn and recall both duration and order differs from most historical and contemporary models of sequence learning.
source: The ability of the network to internally learn and recall both duration and order, along with its use of a local learning rule that bypasses the need for constant and explicit targets, differs from most historical and contemporary models of sequence learning (Fiete et al., 2010; Pereira and Brunel, 2019; Klos et al., 2018; Jun and Jin, 2007; Liu and Buonomano, 2009; Maes et al., 2020; Murray and Escola, 2017; Martinez et al., 2019; Rajan et al., 2016; DePasquale et al., 2018; Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Sussillo and Abbott, 2009; Nicola and Clopath, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to cited models.

claim: Chain structure models of neural sequence learning operate in a method akin to synfire chains.
source: Chain structure models of neural sequence learning operate in a method akin to synfire chains (Abeles, 1991) – that is, representations of different individual stimuli are linked together, in order, via feed-forward synaptic connections (Fiete et al., 2010; Pereira and Brunel, 2019; Klos et al., 2018; Jun and Jin, 2007; Liu and Buonomano, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant models.

claim: Chain-like structures can readily encode order but do not internally encode start times, stop times, or durations of individual elements.
source: While such a chain-like structure can readily encode order, there is nothing internally encoding start times, stop times, or durations of the individual elements of the sequence.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of chain-like models.

claim: Some chain models use the resulting activity chain as a temporal basis or 'clock' upon which elements and their durations can be learned at the level of the output.
source: Some models use the resulting activity chain as a temporal basis or 'clock', upon which elements and their durations can be learned at the level of the output, but the fragility of the chain itself can make such output representations very sensitive to noise (Liu and Buonomano, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific model.

claim: The fragility of activity chains can make output representations very sensitive to noise.
source: Some models use the resulting activity chain as a temporal basis or 'clock', upon which elements and their durations can be learned at the level of the output, but the fragility of the chain itself can make such output representations very sensitive to noise (Liu and Buonomano, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific model.

claim: RNNs learn complex sequences by leveraging rich, dynamical representations to approximate target outputs.
source: Unlike explicit feed-forward chain models, RNNs learn complex sequences by leveraging rich, dynamical representations to approximate target outputs.
evidence: This is a general characterization of RNN models based on established knowledge.

claim: RNNs are fully capable of encoding duration and order.
source: RNNs are fully capable of encoding duration and order, and can embed multiple sequences at once.
evidence: This is a general characterization of RNN capabilities based on established knowledge.

claim: Common learning rules for RNNs, such as backpropagation through time or FORCE, are biologically unrealistic.
source: However, common learning rules for these models, such as backpropagation through time (BPTT) or FORCE, are biologically unrealistic, as they require some combination of non-local information, precise and symmetrical feedback structures, and/or explicit feedback about the targets at every time point (Whittington and Bogacz, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and established knowledge about biological plausibility.

claim: Networks can under some conditions learn inputs via random feedback connections rather than backpropagation.
source: Interestingly, recent work has shown that networks can under some conditions learn inputs via random feedback connections rather than backpropagation (Lillicrap et al., 2016), but this random feedback is less effective than BPTT for learning sequences with long time scales (Murray, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Random feedback is less effective than BPTT for learning sequences with long time scales.
source: Interestingly, recent work has shown that networks can under some conditions learn inputs via random feedback connections rather than backpropagation (Lillicrap et al., 2016), but this random feedback is less effective than BPTT for learning sequences with long time scales (Murray, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The expression of sequences in the brain often follows a compressed encoding, in which order is represented but duration is not.
source: Experimentally, the expression of sequences in the brain often follows a compressed encoding, in which order is represented but duration is not, and sequences are replayed with a time scale dictated by the intrinsic time scales of the circuit (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Davidson et al., 2009; Ji and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: There are many cases where neural sequences are learned and replayed at or near their behavioral time scale.
source: However, there are also many cases where neural sequences are learned and replayed at or near their behavioral time scale (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Louie and Wilson, 2001; Eichenlaub et al., 2020; Dave and Margoliash, 2000), for which a simple ordered chain is insufficient.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model's chain-like, modular structure enables it to learn the order of elements.
source: Our model's chain-like, modular structure enables it learn the order of elements, while the recurrent structure within that chain allows it to internally and flexibly learn those elements' duration.
evidence: This is a description of how the model architecture enables specific functions.

claim: The recurrent structure within the chain allows the model to internally and flexibly learn elements' duration.
source: Our model's chain-like, modular structure enables it learn the order of elements, while the recurrent structure within that chain allows it to internally and flexibly learn those elements' duration.
evidence: This is a description of how the model architecture enables specific functions.

claim: The structure of the network allows the use of a local, biophysically realistic learning rule to adjust the synaptic weights.
source: The structure of our network allows us to use a local, biophysically realistic learning rule to adjust the synaptic weights.
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism.

claim: A transient sequential input is presented during training.
source: A transient sequential input is presented during training, and over the course of training, our learning rule causes the weights to reach fixed points.
evidence: This describes the training procedure used in the model.

claim: Over the course of training, the learning rule causes the weights to reach fixed points.
source: A transient sequential input is presented during training, and over the course of training, our learning rule causes the weights to reach fixed points.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the learning rule during training, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: After training, the network can recall the uncompressed transient activity of the sequential input upon only partial reactivation.
source: After training, the network can then recall the uncompressed transient activity of the sequential input, complete with both duration and order, upon only partial reactivation (e.g. stimulating only the first element in the sequence).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3e.

claim: In a traditional 'chain-like' network with Hebbian learning, order of presented stimuli can be readily encoded by learning directional feed-forward connections between populations.
source: In a traditional 'chain-like' network with Hebbian learning, order of presented stimuli can be readily encoded by learning directional feed-forward connections between populations.
evidence: This is a general statement about chain-like networks based on established knowledge.

claim: A simple chain architecture is insufficient for internally representing the duration of presented stimuli and their specific start and end times.
source: However, this simple architecture proves insufficient for internally representing the duration of presented stimuli and their specific start and end times, as intrinsic time constants determine the speed at which the signal travels through the network (Murray and Escola, 2017; Martinez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Intrinsic time constants determine the speed at which the signal travels through a chain network.
source: However, this simple architecture proves insufficient for internally representing the duration of presented stimuli and their specific start and end times, as intrinsic time constants determine the speed at which the signal travels through the network (Murray and Escola, 2017; Martinez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The network of spiking neurons can learn the order, duration, and specific timing of sequence elements.
source: In this work we present a network of spiking neurons that can learn the order, duration, and specific timing of sequence elements.
evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the Results section, particularly in Figures 3-5.

claim: The model uses local and biophysically realistic learning rules, in contrast to most RNN models.
source: This model uses local and biophysically realistic learning rules, in contrast to most RNN models (DePasquale et al., 2018; Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Sussillo and Abbott, 2009; Nicola and Clopath, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to cited RNN models.

claim: In the model, order is learned by modifying the feed-forward synaptic efficacies between modules.
source: As in the 'chain-like' models, the order is learned by modifying the feed-forward synaptic efficacies between modules.
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: The duration of each element is learned via modification of the recurrent connections within each module.
source: Unlike those models, the duration of each element is learned via modification of the recurrent connections within each module (Fiete et al., 2010; Pereira and Brunel, 2019; Klos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Additional structure within each module and in the allowed connections between modules allows the model to avoid compression during recall while using relatively simple local learning rules.
source: In order to solve this problem, we assume additional structure within each module and in the allowed connections between modules. This additional structure allows us to avoid compression during recall while using relatively simple local learning rules.
evidence: This is a description of how the model architecture enables specific functions.

claim: The cellular response types generated by this network are consistent with experimental observation.
source: Consequently, the cellular response types generated by this network are consistent with experimental observation (Shuler and Bear, 2006; Liu et al., 2015), as described below.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is shown in Figure 2.

claim: The network is composed of different modules that are selectively activated via feed-forward connections by different external stimuli.
source: Our network is composed of different modules that are selectively activated via feed-forward connections by different external stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Within each module, there are two populations of excitatory cells as well as inhibitory cells.
source: Within each module, there are two populations of excitatory cells as well as inhibitory cells (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The excitatory cells in both populations are identical in their intrinsic properties but differ in their learned and fixed connections with other cells.
source: The excitatory cells in both populations are identical in their intrinsic properties but differ in their learned and fixed connections with other cells within the module and in different modules.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: Timer cells learn strong recurrent connections with other Timer cells within the module.
source: The 'Timer' cells learn strong recurrent connections with other Timer cells within the module.
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Strong recurrent connectivity in Timer cells results in long-lasting transient activity, which is used to represent the duration of a given stimuli.
source: This strong recurrent connectivity results in long-lasting transient activity, which is used to represent the duration of a given stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of how the model represents duration, as shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Previous studies have analyzed in detail the relationship between recurrent connectivity and duration of resulting transient activity following a stimulus.
source: Previous studies have analyzed in detail the relationship between recurrent connectivity and duration of resulting transient activity following a stimulus (Gavornik et al., 2009; Gavornik and Shouval, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Timers excite the inhibitory cells and the Messenger cells.
source: Timers also excite the inhibitory cells and the 'Messenger' cells.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Inhibitory cells have roughly the same temporal profile as Timers but decay slightly more quickly.
source: Since the inhibitory cells receive input from the Timers, they have roughly the same temporal profile. However, inhibitory cells in the module decay slightly more quickly than their Timer counterparts, thanks to a combination of shorter time constants for synaptic activation (80 ms for excitatory, 10 ms for inhibitory), and small Timer to inhibitory weights (there are a number of degenerate sets of parameters which can facilitate quickly decaying inhibitory cells) (Huertas et al., 2015) (see 'Materials and methods' and Supplementary materials for more details).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture and dynamics, as shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Messenger cells selectively fire at the end of the Timers' transient activity.
source: Owing to this temporal offset, Messenger cells selectively fire at the end of the Timers' transient activity, since they receive input from both the Timer cells and the (faster decaying) inhibitory cells.
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics, as shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The temporally specific profile of the Messenger cells enables them to convey a temporally specific transition between elements.
source: The temporally specific profile of the Messenger cells enables them to convey a temporally specific transition between elements, via learned feed-forward connections to Timer cells in other modules.
evidence: This is a description of how the model architecture enables specific functions.

claim: The Timer/inhibitory/Messenger modular architecture can be constructed in a number of redundant ways, including simply via random distributions of connections.
source: The Timer/inhibitory/Messenger modular architecture can be constructed in a number of redundant ways, including simply via random distributions of connections (see previous work (Huertas et al., 2015) for a more detailed analysis).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The learning rule is based on two competing, synapse-specific, Hebbian-activated eligibility traces: one for long-term potentiation (LTP) and one for long-term depression (LTD).
source: For learning, we use a previously described reinforcement learning rule based on two competing, synapse-specific, Hebbian-activated eligibility traces (Huertas et al., 2016; He et al., 2015): one for long-term potentiation (LTP) and one for long-term depression (LTD) (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a description of the learning rule used in the model, supported by citations.

claim: The presence of Hebbian activity at a given synapse activates the two traces at different rates and to different saturation levels.
source: The presence of Hebbian activity at a given synapse activates the two traces at different rates (and to different saturation levels), and the absence of Hebbian activity causes the traces to decay at different rates.
evidence: This is a description of the learning rule dynamics.

claim: The change in synaptic weight is determined by the difference in eligibility traces upon presentation of a reinforcement signal.
source: The change in synaptic weight is determined simply by the difference in these traces upon presentation of a reinforcement signal.
evidence: This is a description of the learning rule, as shown in Equation 14.

claim: On every transition between external stimuli, a 'novelty' signal causes a global release of a neuromodulator, which acts as a reinforcement signal.
source: We have assumed that on every transition between external stimuli, a 'novelty' signal causes a global release of a neuromodulator, which acts as a reinforcement signal (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism.

claim: The assumption of a temporally precise but spatially widespread neuromodulatory signal is consistent with recent recordings in several neuromodulatory systems.
source: The assumption of a temporally precise but spatially widespread neuromodulatory signal might seem at odds with common notions of temporally broad neuromodulator release, but they are indeed consistent with recent recordings in several neruomodulatory systems (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Hangya et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Eligibility traces for LTP have been found in multiple brain regions.
source: Eligibility traces for LTP have been found in multiple brain regions (Yagishita et al., 2014; Bittner et al., 2017; Brzosko et al., 2017), and eligibility traces for both LTP and LTD have been found in both visual and prefrontal cortex (He et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Eligibility traces for both LTP and LTD have been found in both visual and prefrontal cortex.
source: Eligibility traces for LTP have been found in multiple brain regions (Yagishita et al., 2014; Bittner et al., 2017; Brzosko et al., 2017), and eligibility traces for both LTP and LTD have been found in both visual and prefrontal cortex (He et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: The eligibility trace learning rule can solve the temporal credit assignment problem.
source: We have used this rule because it can solve the temporal credit assignment problem, allowing the network to associate events distal in time, and because it reaches fixed points in both recurrent and feed-forward learning tasks (Huertas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The eligibility trace learning rule reaches fixed points in both recurrent and feed-forward learning tasks.
source: We have used this rule because it can solve the temporal credit assignment problem, allowing the network to associate events distal in time, and because it reaches fixed points in both recurrent and feed-forward learning tasks (Huertas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Using the described rule and architecture within a single module, the network naturally generates cells that learn to be active for the duration of the stimulus (Timers) and other cells that activate toward the end of the stimulus duration (Messengers).
source: Using this rule and the described architecture within a single module, we find (Figure 2a) that the network naturally generates cells that learn to be active for the duration of the stimulus (Timers), and other cells that activate toward the end of the stimulus duration (Messengers).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2a.

claim: Timer cells learn the duration of the stimulus via changes in the excitatory synaptic efficacies within the Timer population.
source: The Timer cells learn the duration of the stimulus via changes in the excitatory synaptic efficacies within the Timer population.
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Messenger cells evolve their specific temporal profile due to the temporal profiles of their fixed excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the Timer cells and the inhibitory cells.
source: The Messenger cells evolve their specific temporal profile due to the temporal profiles of their fixed excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the Timer cells and the inhibitory cells.
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics, as shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The model results are consistent with experimental observations in V1 circuits that learn the duration between a stimulus and a reward.
source: These results are consistent with experimental observations in V1 circuits that learn the duration between a stimulus and a reward (Shuler and Bear, 2006; Liu et al., 2015; Chubykin et al., 2013), as shown in Figure 2b.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and comparison to Figure 2b.

claim: The model results replicate previous results using a learning rule with a single trace.
source: These results replicate our previous results (Huertas et al., 2015) which used a learning rule with a single trace (Gavornik et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The modular microcircuit acts as a 'core neural architecture' (CNA), an elemental package of basic temporal neural responses.
source: This modular microcircuit, in which both Timer and Messenger cells emerge from learning, acts as a 'core neural architecture' (CNA) (Huertas et al., 2015), an elemental package of basic temporal neural responses which can then be used within the larger network to create more complicated representations.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture, supported by citation.

claim: The CNA functions as the basic microcircuit for the sequence model.
source: This CNA functions as the basic microcircuit for our sequence model, and each 'element' of an input sequence is represented by one of these CNA circuits.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: The individual CNAs are plastic, as their temporal properties are not fixed but adapt to the environment through recurrent learning in the Timer population.
source: One must note that the individual CNAs are plastic, as their temporal properties are not fixed but adapt to the environment, through recurrent learning in the Timer population.
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism.

claim: The model places distinct CNAs sensitive to particular visual stimuli in a columnar structure.
source: In a structure akin to the microcircuits found in cortical columns (Potjans and Diesmann, 2014), this model places distinct CNAs sensitive to particular visual stimuli in a columnar structure, as shown in Figure 3a.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 3a, supported by citation.

claim: There is soft winner-take-all (WTA) inhibition between the columns to prevent spurious excitation in the noisy, spiking network.
source: To prevent spurious excitation in our noisy, spiking network, there is soft winner-take-all (WTA) inhibition between the columns (see 'Materials and methods' and 'Discussion' for more details).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: When presenting a sequence of visual stimuli, different CNAs in turn become activated in sequence.
source: When presenting a sequence of visual stimuli, different CNAs in turn become activated in sequence.
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Timer cells within CNAs learn the duration of their particular stimuli via recurrent connections.
source: Timer cells within those CNAs learn the duration of their particular stimuli via recurrent connections, while order is learned via feed-forward connections from Messengers in one column to Timers in a subsequently presented column.
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Order is learned via feed-forward connections from Messengers in one column to Timers in a subsequently presented column.
source: Timer cells within those CNAs learn the duration of their particular stimuli via recurrent connections, while order is learned via feed-forward connections from Messengers in one column to Timers in a subsequently presented column.
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: The modular architecture can overcome the problem of sequence compression encountered by 'chain-like' models.
source: We will show that this modular architecture can overcome the problem of sequence compression encountered by 'chain-like' models.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3e, where the network recalls the sequence without compression.

claim: The network is capable of robustly learning sequences of temporal intervals.
source: Using the above described architecture and learning rule (see 'Materials and methods' for more details), the network is capable of robustly learning sequences of temporal intervals.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3-5.

claim: Figure 3 shows the network learning a sequence of four different elements, of duration 500, 1000, 700, and 1800 ms.
source: Figure 3 shows the network learning a sequence of four different elements, of duration 500, 1000, 700, and 1800 ms.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: The inputs are modeled after lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) responses to spot stimuli.
source: In this example, the inputs are modeled after lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) responses to spot stimuli (Ruksenas et al., 2007; Mastronarde, 1987, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but more generally one may consider these stimuli to be oriented gratings, specific natural images in a movie, or non-visual stimuli such as pitches of sounds in a song.
evidence: This is a description of the model inputs, supported by citations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Before learning, presentation of the blue stimulus only produces a transient response in the CNA microcircuit housed in the blue-sensitive column.
source: Before learning, presentation of the blue stimulus only produces a transient response in the CNA microcircuit housed in the blue-sensitive column (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3b.

claim: During learning, a sequence of stimuli is presented, and microcircuits in their respective columns learn to represent the duration of the stimulus which activates them.
source: During learning (Figure 3c,d), a sequence of stimuli is presented, and microcircuits in their respective columns learn to represent the duration of the stimulus which activates them.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: The different microcircuits learn to 'chain' together in the order in which they were stimulated.
source: The different microcircuits also learn to 'chain' together in the order in which they were stimulated.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: After learning, presentation of the blue stimulus triggers a 'recall' of the entire sequence.
source: After learning, presentation of the blue stimulus triggers a 'recall' of the entire sequence (Figure 3e): blue for 500 ms, red for 1000 ms, green for 700 ms, and orange for 1800 ms.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3e.

claim: The network is capable of learning sequences of temporal intervals where the individual elements can be anywhere from ~300 to ~1800 ms in duration.
source: The network is capable of learning sequences of temporal intervals where the individual elements can be anywhere from ~300 to ~1800 ms (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2) in duration, which agrees with the observed ranges used for training V1 circuits (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Shuler and Bear, 2006).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and supported by citations.

claim: The network itself shows realistic spiking statistics, with interspike interval coefficients (ISIs) of variation near 1.
source: The network itself shows realistic spiking statistics, with interspike interval coefficients (ISIs) of variation near 1.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The resulting firing rates are roughly consistent with the experimentally observed Timers and Messengers.
source: The resulting firing rates are also roughly consistent with the experimentally observed Timers and Messengers (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison to Figure 2.

claim: In simulations, the network has been able to learn a sequence of up to eight elements.
source: In simulations we have been able to learn a sequence of up to eight elements (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The upper limit on the number of elements which can be learned in a sequence has not been fully explored due to the computational time required.
source: The upper limit on the number of elements which can be learned in a sequence has not been fully explored due to the computational time required.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: Sequences of four elements were chosen to match experimental results.
source: For this work, sequences of four elements were chosen to match experimental results (Gavornik and Bear, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the design choices of the study, supported by citation.

claim: Similar results are obtained with a low dimensional rate model in which the activity of each population is presented by a single dynamical variable.
source: The model presented here is a high dimensional spiking model, but similar results are obtained with a low dimensional rate model in which the activity of each population is presented by a single dynamical variable (for details, see 'Materials and methods' and Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Before training, presentation of an isolated stimulus only evokes a transient response of the CNA sensitive to that specific stimulus.
source: Before training, presentation of an isolated stimulus only evokes a transient response of the CNA sensitive to that specific stimulus, since the Timer cells have yet to learn any recurrent connections, and the Messenger cells have yet to establish any feed-forward connections to the Timer cells in other columns (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4a.

claim: During training, a particular sequence of inputs is presented and then repeated over many trials.
source: During training, a particular sequence of inputs is presented and then repeated over many trials.
evidence: This is a description of the training procedure.

claim: Hebbian activity in the network triggers activation of synapse-specific LTP and LTD associated eligibility traces.
source: Hebbian activity in the network triggers activation of synapse-specific LTP and LTD associated eligibility traces, which are then converted into changes in synaptic connections upon neuromodulator release (purple arrows in Figure 4), occurring here closely after a change in stimuli (see Equations 8, 9, and 14 in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a description of the learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Each trial pushes the weights in the network toward their fixed points.
source: Each trial pushes the weights in the network toward their fixed points (Equations 17 and 18 in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a description of the learning dynamics, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Hebbian activity within the Timer population causes activation of their respective eligibility traces, and subsequently an increase in their recurrent connections.
source: Hebbian activity within the Timer population causes activation of their respective eligibility traces, and subsequently an increase in their recurrent connections (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: As lateral connections grow, Timer cells sustain their activity for longer, 'extending' their firing profile out in time toward the neuromodulator signal associated with the start of the subsequent stimulus.
source: As these lateral connections grow, Timer cells sustain their activity for longer, 'extending' their firing profile out in time toward the neuromodulator signal associated with the start of the subsequent stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the learning dynamics, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: As Timer cells extend their activity, Messenger cells get 'dragged' along, eventually coactivating with Timer cells of the column which is stimulated next.
